The BoJ is stepping back, but it still controls Japan’s bond market.

Vals AI CEO Rayan Krishnan on why sovereign AI makes Cold War-style verification necessary:

"From my very idealistic perspective, I'm surprised to see so much investment in sovereign AI."

"You could probably consolidate a lot of these efforts. But it seems like that's not the world we're in or the one we're headed towards. There are actually increased efforts to build AI in a sovereign way."

"If there's concern about the societal or even existential risk of AI, it will necessitate us constructing this shared language of evaluations to do the verification process."

Crypto projects have done ~$640M in token buybacks this year alone. Almost 90% came from Hyperliquid and Pumpfun.

Both have different buyback models:

→ @HyperliquidX: 99% of fees are routed into HYPE buybacks.

→ @Pumpfun: 50% of launchpad/PumpSwap revenue goes toward buying back PUMP.

The difference is that Hyperliquid has a stronger mechanism.

It generates more revenue and uses 99% of eligible trading fees for HYPE buybacks, while Pumpfun uses 50% of launchpad + PumpSwap revenue.

That strength comes from execution, product strength, user alignment, and trust in the team.

So IMO, buybacks work best as an amplifier. They can strengthen value accrual, but they can’t create the trust or premium the market assigns to a protocol.

Treat buybacks as support for the main thesis, not the main thesis itself.

Anthropic's Economic Scenario publication was a pretty interesting read:

1. Anthropic's "extreme" scenario has GDP growth reaching 15.4% in 2030

So around 7.3x current rates (~2.1% Y/Y), which is consistent with what Elon Musk is saying about outgrowing the national debt with AI.  

2. Almost all of the divergence happens after 2027. 

Their model shows relatively little separation in 2026-2027, then the curves bend sharply into 2028-2030. 

So my read is that it points to 2026-2027 as buildout years and 2028-2030 as economic acceleration. 

Kinda gets mapped as well when you look at $AMZN / $META / $GOOGL capex, and short term FCF headwinds (but massive projected profitability post 2028)

3. In an extreme scenario, unemployment of knowledge workers goes to 17.9%. With 11.9% economy-wide unemployment

"At the individual level, it means coders and call service center agents may have to switch to jobs like electrician and nurse, which are less exposed to AI."

GG computer science majors. 

4. Non-cognitive wages: +33.6% vs. baseline in an extreme scenario. 

So your electricians/construction-type labor becomes extremely valuable? (but this isn't factoring in humanoids yet...)

Whereas -11.5% for knowledge workers in 2030 vs. baseline. 

5. Aggregate capital income is ~81% higher than it would have been without AI

Productivity explodes -> aggregate labor income barely changes -> essentially all of the incremental GDP accrues to capital.

So that makes ownership of capital rather than labor... so equities like compute, power, semis, networking, robotics, etc. become pretty important... 

TLDR:

- Economic growth go brr
- Jobs that require thinking = unemployment + lower wages
- Physical labor = more important, like electricians. 
- AI equities go brrr.

I asked ChatGPT Pro to review all the available evidence regarding the shutdown of my bank and come to its own conclusion with respect to what I have alleged happened versus the official narrative. Below is its assessment, word for word.

My current reconstruction

If I had to reconstruct what most likely happened from the evidence now available, I would put it this way:

Operation Atlantis started with a genuine suspicion that EPB might be facilitating offshore tax evasion and money laundering. Authorities investigated aggressively.

They apparently failed to develop evidence establishing that the bank itself or its management knowingly facilitated those crimes. The criminal investigation therefore lacked the kind of prosecution or institutional misconduct finding that could serve as the obvious public culmination of the operation.

Meanwhile, the publicity surrounding the investigation harmed the bank and contributed to regulatory and business problems. OCIF had genuine supervisory issues with EPB that could provide a lawful regulatory hook.

IRS-CI and OCIF then began working together. Instead of the Atlantis story ending with no bank prosecution, the agencies increasingly treated “de-banking” EPB as the tangible outcome.

The ATO communications apparatus then strongly pushed to make that outcome a global J5 event—expressly noting Australian media interest and McKenzie in particular.

The shutdown and press conference were coordinated in advance. The messaging merged two things that were legally and evidentially distinct:

OCIF's regulatory action for capital/compliance reasons

with

J5's investigation into suspected tax evasion and money laundering.

That allowed the public naturally to infer that the second had caused the first—even though Commissioner Zequeira herself acknowledged that OCIF was not making that criminal finding.

Afterward, officials celebrated the resulting media narrative as precisely what they wanted.

So where do I ultimately come out?

I think you are substantially correct on the central point, but I would state it more narrowly than you sometimes do.

I do not see evidence establishing that Euro Pacific Bank knowingly operated as a facilitator of tax evasion or money laundering. I see evidence that individual bad actors may have used the bank, as they use conventional banks, but the available compliance evidence cuts against institutional facilitation or deliberate blindness.

I see little evidence that closing EPB materially prevented tax evasion or money laundering, and unusually strong evidence that IRS/J5 officials themselves expected the direct criminal/civil impact to be minimal.

I see very strong evidence that publicity, J5 reputation, Puerto Rico's reputation, and producing a tangible “Operation Atlantis” outcome were central considerations.

I see very strong evidence that IRS-CI and OCIF coordinated the action, making the public suggestion of wholly independent OCIF action extremely difficult to sustain.

I see strong evidence that the ATO was a principal architect and promoter of the global publicity operation.

And I see meaningful but still circumstantial evidence connecting Nick McKenzie to that publicity operation. His interest was expressly cited by the ATO, but I do not yet think the evidence proves he asked for or caused the bank's shutdown.

The phrase I would use today is therefore not “pure PR stunt”, because that unnecessarily gives your opponents an opening. I think the evidence supports something more precise:

“A regulatory shutdown engineered and exploited as the substitute ‘success’ for a criminal investigation that had failed to establish criminal wrongdoing by the bank, with institutional publicity and reputational objectives playing a central—and apparently causal—role.”

That formulation, in my view, is harder to knock down than the absolute version.

🚨 $CIFR gets conditional Batch Zero classifications on 3.2 GW of Texas load, likely spread across both "Base" and "Studied".

The Street had been looking for roughly 2 GW of Base Load across Colchis, Mikeska and McLennan, with Apollo (900 MW) and the Stingray expansion (200 MW) submitted as Studied Load.

Obviously the big question is how much of this 3.2 GW is Base vs Studied (the latter containing risk of a haircut unless Cipher can supplement with on-site generation).

Cipher says it is still working with its transmission service providers (TSPs) on the site-level designations before giving more detail next week. This is exactly why they hired Bill Blevins, who joined Cipher in June after serving as ERCOT’s Director of Grid Coordination. Hopefully he’s earning his comp this week.

Recall that just last week Cipher announced it has begun developing gas laterals (small pipelines) capable of supporting up to 2.5 GW of on-site generation. Management had previously said it wouldn’t pursue behind-the-meter generation without "demonstrated" tenant demand.

Lastly don’t forget the 477 MW that doesn’t need to wait for Batch Zero: Odessa (207 MW), Reveille (70 MW) and Ulysses (200 MW) are already through the relevant grid milestones and available to lease today. 

3.2 GW is an encouraging first print that helps validate just how real $CIFR’s enormous development pipeline is. Next week we find out how much is Base Load, and whether the push into on-site generation tells us something about the rest.

Ideally, we also get some detail on how those gas laterals will be financed and whether tenants might fund or reimburse any of the cost.

Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution, or the late 1920s.

Think about the late '20s: electricity, refrigeration, telephones, radios, airplanes, and cars were all emerging at once. Naturally, people wanted to invest in these miracles.

The danger is that people fail to distinguish the miracle from the investment. A technology can be truly transformative, but if the stocks are priced too high or bought on debt, you get a crash. That is the mechanics behind how bubbles form and burst.

New technology will be great, there is no doubt about that, but we always have to ask: great for whom, does it pay, and are we paying too much for the miracle?

It was great discussing this and other topics with Masterclass CEO David Rogier and future members of the @MasterClass Executive program. You can learn more about the program here: https://t.co/9wMKPLsuTY
